name: Lakshmi Devi
headline: 71-year-old water quality monitor in Karnataka
description:
Lakshmi Devi’s hands are never still. When she walks the six kilometres from her village to the river bend and back, she carries a blue plastic bucket in one hand and a bamboo staff in the other. The bucket holds samples—water from hand pumps, from shallow wells, from the ditch where children sometimes play. She wraps each sample in a length of old sari to keep it cool, and on the return leg she stops at every pump to wipe the rim with a clean cloth before filling her container. Her movements are slow but precise; she has done this every day for eighteen months. At the university laboratory, the students tease her gently: ‘Lakshmi-ma’am, you bring us cleaner water than we can collect ourselves.’ She laughs, but does not slow down.

She was born in the same village, the youngest of five daughters. Her first memory is of the communal tap—a rusted iron pipe that ran for two hours in the morning and two hours at dusk. She carried a brass lota to school, then a plastic jerrycan after she married and moved to her husband’s home. Her husband, a weaver, died of kidney failure when their youngest child was twelve. The doctors said it might have been the water. Lakshmi does not know for sure, but she remembers the way his ankles swelled, the smell of the village pond in the dry season.

Her children now live in the city—a son who sells mobile phones, a daughter who works in a call centre. They call every Sunday and beg her to move. She tells them she has work to do. ‘The university people need me,’ she says, though really it is the other way around. She has learned to read the colour chart for arsenic strips, to record coordinates in a thick notebook with a pencil tied to a string. She argues with the younger field assistants about which wells to prioritise. They want statistical coverage; she wants every hand pump that a child might drink from.

She believes, with a clarity that surprises even herself, that water can be made clean. Not through prayer alone—she still lights a lamp every morning—but through patience, through walking, through testing each drop one by one. When people ask why she bothers at her age, she says, ‘I am not too old to carry water. I have carried it all my life. Now I carry the truth of it.’
